questions.q: What does std::thread's constructor do when you pass it a callable and arguments?
options: It starts the new thread running immediately and returns right away
It schedules the thread to start only after join() is called
It runs the callable synchronously on the calling thread first
It compiles the callable into a separate executable
questions.explain: A std::thread begins executing concurrently as soon as it's constructed; the constructor does not block waiting for it to finish.

questions.q: What happens if a std::thread object representing a still-running thread is destroyed without join() or detach() being called?
options: The thread is silently detached for you
The program calls std::terminate and crashes
The destructor blocks forever waiting for the thread
Nothing — the thread simply continues in the background
questions.explain: A joinable std::thread whose destructor runs without join() or detach() having been called terminates the program.

questions.q: Why does `trade_count = trade_count + 1;` cause a data race when run concurrently by two threads without synchronization?
options: Because addition is undefined for the long type
Because it is really a read, an add, and a write — three steps that can interleave between threads
Because std::thread cannot access global variables
Because the compiler refuses to compile shared globals
questions.explain: The statement decomposes into read-modify-write. If two threads interleave those steps, one thread can read a stale value and overwrite the other's update, losing an increment.

questions.q: According to the C++ standard, what is the consequence of a data race?
options: A guaranteed, deterministic wrong answer
A compiler warning, but correct behavior at runtime
Undefined behavior — the compiler may assume races never happen
A guaranteed crash with a clear error message
questions.explain: The C++ standard defines a data race as undefined behavior. The compiler is permitted to optimize under the assumption that no data races occur, so results are not just "wrong" but unpredictable.

questions.q: Why can't a passing test run prove that threaded code is free of data races?
options: Because unit test frameworks cannot compile multithreaded code
Because data races depend on the OS thread scheduler's timing, which varies between runs and environments
Because std::thread disables optimizations during testing
Because data races only occur on multi-socket servers
questions.explain: Thread scheduling is effectively nondeterministic from the program's point of view, so a race might not manifest on one run (or one machine) yet reliably corrupt data under different timing or load.
